The River darter (Percina shumardi) attains a maximum recorded total length of 10 cm [Li = 10 cm] based on field surveys throughout the Mississippi River drainage, with individuals reaching this upper size limit primarily in larger, free-flowing river habitats. Neonates emerge from demersal, adhesive eggs after an incubation period, and the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.0009 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0009 grams], a value derived from the average egg diameter of 1.2 mm measured in gravid females collected from the Ohio River system. This minute initial mass places the species among the smaller-bodied percids and reflects the typical constraints of producing relatively large, nutrient-rich oocytes relative to the female's body size.

Puberty in Percina shumardi is reached at a standard length of 4.8 cm [Lp = 4.8 cm], a size threshold that corresponds closely with the attainment of one year of age based on otolith-derived growth curves from populations in the Tennessee River. At this size, individuals undergo gonadal recrudescence and initiate vitellogenesis, entering the reproductively viable life stage. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 0.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.7 grams], a body mass that represents a substantial investment in somatic growth prior to the onset of reproductive activity.

This high fecundity, facilitated by a batch-spawning strategy, allows the species to exploit seasonally abundant food resources in its sandy to gravelly riverine habitats.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Percina shumardi is approximately 7 grams [Wwi = approximately 7 grams], corresponding to the asymptotic body mass derived from length-weight regressions based on extensive collections across the species' range. This body mass falls within the typical range for small-bodied darters of the genus, consistent with its benthic foraging ecology. The length-weight relationship follows a strong allometric curve that is characteristic of darters occupying flowing-water habitats, where streamlined body shapes are favored.

Maximum lifespan in the River darter has been documented from mark-recapture studies in the upper Mississippi River, where the oldest individuals persist for approximately 1275 days [am = approximately 1275 days] under the prevailing thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This longevity, equivalent to roughly 3.5 years, is characteristic of a relatively fast-paced life history among darters, with most individuals likely succumbing to natural mortality from predation or habitat disturbance before reaching this upper boundary. The moderate lifespan facilitates multiple spawning seasons for iteroparous females, contributing to the species' demographic resilience in dynamic riverine environments.
